The bus to school was cancelled because the road had flooded, so everyone in Manjula's lane had to walk the long way through the rain. Her friend Shreya had a fever, and the girl could barely keep up.
Manjula, ten, took Shreya's heavy bag without asking and hung it on her own front, so she looked like a turtle with two shells. Water splashed over her sandals. Her shoulders ached.
"You'll get tired," Shreya said weakly.
"I'm fine. Hold the umbrella."
At the school gate, Kusum's gang ran up. "Shreya, is it true you sleep with a toy rabbit? Manjula knows. Tell us, Manjula!"
Shreya had told her that on a sleepover, whispering. Manjula's face went hot. "I don't know anything," she said, and walked Shreya straight to the sick room.

At lunch the whole table guessed. "Vasudha, you know, don't you? Your face says so!"
Vasudha bit into her chapati and shrugged. Under the table, Parul squeezed her hand.

I'm Kashish, and looking back at my first month in Hyderabad, I remember how lost I felt. I'd come from Shillong, a skinny boy of eighteen, for my engineering course. The food was different, the heat was different, and at night the flat was so quiet I could hear my own homesickness.
I didn't tell anyone. But Sachin, my flatmate, must have noticed I'd stopped eating dinner. One night he knocked with two mugs of ginger tea and said, "Old cricket highlights?" He sat on my floor for an hour. He didn't ask what was wrong.
The next night he did it again. And the next. Once he brought a packet of chips from the only shop that stocked the kind we have back home.
By the end of that week, the flat didn't feel like a stranger's place anymore. I still missed home. But now there was a knock I could count on, and that made me feel I belonged there.

qa.q: What did Sachin bring on the first night?
qa.a: Two mugs of ginger tea.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel once Sachin's knock became a nightly thing?
qa.a: He felt safer and less alone; the flat stopped feeling like a stranger's place, and he felt he belonged there.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's choices mattered most to Kashish, and why?
qa.a: Coming back every night without asking what was wrong mattered most, because the steady small kindness showed Kashish he could count on someone.

qa.q: How might Sachin have seen Kashish during that first month?
qa.a: Sachin probably noticed a quiet flatmate who had stopped eating and guessed he was struggling, choosing company over questions.

grounding: It shows a homesick student whose flatmate brings tea and time every night without being asked, and who comes to feel safe and that he belongs.

"Parveen Apa, just tonight? Please?" Imran stood in the doorway with his baby son on his hip. "We have Rubina's cousin's wedding. You're so good with him."
Parveen was still in her office clothes, her feet aching. "Imran, I babysat Tuesday and Thursday. I've been up since five."
"But you always say yes."
"I know." She took a breath. "And that's why I'm saying no tonight. If I keep saying yes when I'm this tired, I'll start snapping at you all, and I don't want that."
Imran's face fell. "So what do I do?"
"Ask Ammi. Or take him along; he sleeps anywhere." She reached out and stroked the baby's cheek. "But Saturday morning, I'm free. You two go for breakfast, and I'll keep him till lunch. Properly, happily."
Imran was quiet, then grinned a little. "Properly, happily. Deal."

qa.a: On Saturday morning, till lunch.

qa.q: Why did Parveen take a breath before saying no?
qa.a: She felt the pull to say yes as always, and needed a moment to hold her ground because she was exhausted and worried she would start snapping.

qa.q: What choice did Parveen make, and why is it a caring one?
qa.a: She said no tonight but offered Saturday morning, so her help comes from real energy instead of emptying her until she resents it.

I'm Keerthana, and a year ago I was the friend everyone called, the good girl who never said no. Need a ride to the airport at four? Keerthana. Need someone to cover a shift, fix a CV, babysit a dog? Keerthana. I loved being needed. I'm not ashamed of that.
But last March I got so tired I cried in the office washroom because someone asked me to proofread a two-line email. That scared me.
So I started saying something I'd never said: "Not this week, but I can do next Tuesday." The first time, my hands were sweating. My friend Ayesha just said, "Oh, okay," and found someone else. Nothing broke.
When Ayesha moved flats in June, I was rested, and I spent the whole Sunday packing her kitchen, laughing over her twelve identical mugs. I helped more that day than I would have in a month of exhausted yeses.
I still say yes a lot. Just not to everything.

qa.a: A two-line email.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel the first time she said 'not this week'?
qa.a: She was nervous, with sweating hands, afraid that saying no would upset people or break something.

qa.q: What turning point changed Keerthana's habits, and what did she choose after it?
qa.a: Crying over a tiny request scared her into seeing she was empty, so she began offering later dates instead of always saying yes at once.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have experienced Keerthana's change?
qa.a: Ayesha took the first no easily and later got a rested, cheerful friend who spent a whole Sunday helping her move.

I'm Lalit, ten, the smallest boy in our colony's cricket gang. Last summer something happened in our colony that I still think about.
Santosh's family had just moved from another state, and at home they speak a different language. He sat on the wall every evening watching us play cricket. Nobody picked him. When he asked, one of the older boys said, "You're not from here. Go play with your own people." Some kids laughed.
My stomach felt twisted. Santosh wasn't even my friend yet. But it just wasn't fair. He lives here now, same as us.
I said, "That's not fair. He can bat after me." My voice shook a bit. The older boy rolled his eyes, but he let him.
Santosh hit a four on his first ball. After that, nobody said anything. Now he's on my team every evening.

qa.a: When Lalit said Santosh could bat after him, the older boy let him play, and Santosh became part of the team.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt sitting on the wall before Lalit spoke up?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and lonely, watching the game every evening in a new place where nobody picked him.

PE note, Tuesday. Jahnavi, games teacher, Class 5.
Mira joined us this term; her family runs the travelling fair and she will be with us for two months. In today's handball game, her team kept passing around her. When she called for the ball, one girl said, "She's only here for a bit, why bother?"
Tejas, who is on the other team and barely knows Mira, stopped playing and walked over to me. His ears were red. He said, "Ma'am, that's not fair. She's in our class too. Two months is still our class."

At seven on Sunday morning, the mud along the creek in Mumbai smelled of salt and rot. Raghav, fifteen, was knee-deep in it, planting mangrove saplings with his friend Hemant and thirty other volunteers.
"Why mangroves, though?" Hemant grumbled, slapping a mosquito. "Trees are trees."
"They hold the mud when the sea pushes in," Raghav said. "Our geography sir showed us. Where they cut them, the floods come in worse."
He was thinking about the news from last week: a family in a far-off state sitting on their roof, water all around, an old man holding a radio above his head. Raghav had never been there. But he'd lain awake thinking of that man.
"It's not the same sea," Hemant said.
"Same world, though." Raghav pressed the soil around another sapling. "Everything's connected. The weather, the water. I can't fix that roof. I can do this."

qa.a: Mangrove saplings.

qa.a: He was worried about the flooded family and the old man holding the radio, even though they were strangers far away.

qa.q: What choice has Raghav made about his worry, and why does it make sense to him?
qa.a: He turned it into planting mangroves, because he understands that protecting the coast helps against floods, and it is something he can actually do.

qa.a: Hemant sees it as muddy, mosquito-bitten work with no clear link to far-off floods, until Raghav explains how the world is connected.

Mehak walked around the campus twice, then found Sonali in their room. "I can't skip the lottery for you. Then Farzana doesn't get the room she needs. But I'll help you ask the warden about the second-floor corner room."
Sonali stared at her, hurt. Then she said, slowly, "You'd hate yourself if you did it, wouldn't you?"

I'm Bhupen, twenty-five, and when I look back at the year before last, I laugh at myself a little. I was a young man with strong opinions about everything: climate, equality, how the country should be run. I posted long threads at midnight. I didn't know the name of the woman who swept our lane.

I'm Sarita, I'm eleven, and I used to be the best-behaved girl in Class 6. I never forgot my ID card. I never ran in the corridor. I tied my hair in two plaits exactly like Himani and her friends, because they said one plait looked "weird."
In art, Miss told us to paint any sky. Everyone did orange sunsets. I wanted a purple sky with green clouds. I painted an orange sunset.
